opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I hear that a lot, and I think the framing is a bit slippery. "It's just pattern fitting" sounds like a dismissal, but when you push on it, it's not clear what the alternative is supposed to be. Brains are also learning systems shaped by data, by evolution and by lifetime experience. At some level everything that learns is fitting patterns. The interesting question isn't whether a system fits patterns, it's *which* patterns, at what level of abstraction, and how well they generalize.

Where I think the critique does land is on things like data efficiency and the kind of structure that's built in. A kid sees a handful of examples of a new object and can recognize it from any angle, in any lighting, can reason about what happens if you drop it or push it. Our models historically needed enormous amounts of data to get there, and they'd fail in weird ways out of distribution. That's a real gap. But I'd describe it as a gap in inductive biases, training signal, and the richness of the data, not some categorical difference where humans do "real reasoning" and networks do "mere statistics."

A big part of it, for me, coming from vision, is that humans learn from a fundamentally three-dimensional, embodied, interactive world. We don't learn from a pile of static internet images. We move around, we see objects persist over time, we act and see consequences. So if our models look shallow in certain ways, a lot of that may be because we've been feeding them a flattened version of reality. Give models richer signals, 3D structure, video, interaction, and I think a lot of those supposed "divergences" start to shrink.

And honestly, every few years the goalposts move. People said networks couldn't do compositional generalization, couldn't do in-context learning, couldn't write coherent long-form text, and then scale plus better architectures and data chipped away at each of those. I don't think that means we're done, there are clearly missing pieces, things like persistent memory, grounded world models, really robust planning. But I'm skeptical of arguments that say the approach is doomed in principle because it's "only" learning from data. That's kind of what intelligence is.

r001.rationale: The response argues that brains are also learning systems shaped by data and experience, and says that at some level everything that learns is fitting patterns.

r002.rationale: The response mentions reasoning about objects being dropped or pushed, but it does not distinguish learning orbital patterns from having a causal model of gravity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I hear this a lot, and I think the framing kind of smuggles in an assumption I don't buy. The claim is usually something like: humans reason, deep nets just do pattern matching, therefore they're fundamentally different things. But when you actually push on it, "pattern matching" ends up doing a lot of work in that sentence. What is reasoning, if not recognizing that a situation has a structure you've seen before and applying something you learned from that structure? The line between "it just fit the patterns" and "it understood" is a lot blurrier than people want it to be.

I came up through computer vision, so my intuitions come from that side. In the early days, the critique was: these networks are just memorizing textures, they don't know what a cat is. And there was some truth to that, especially with the datasets we had. But every time someone wrote down a crisp test for what "real understanding" would look like, the models eventually passed it, and then the goalposts moved. That's happened enough times now that I'm pretty skeptical of any argument that says there's a categorical wall.

That said, I don't want to overclaim in the other direction. There are real differences. Humans learn from way less data. A kid doesn't need a million labeled images to know what a dog is. Humans have this body, this continuous stream of experience in the physical world, and a lot of our cognition seems grounded in that. Current models are trained mostly on text and images that someone else produced, which is a weirdly indirect way to learn about the world. So the claim that the learning process diverges from how humans learn, I think that's actually true and interesting. But that's a different claim than "the resulting intelligence is fundamentally not intelligence."

The way I'd put it is: deep learning is a different path up the mountain. It doesn't have to replicate human cognition to get to something that functions like intelligence. Airplanes don't flap their wings. And honestly, the fact that these systems arrive at a lot of the same abstractions we do, from such different inputs, is one of the more surprising things I've seen in my career. It suggests a lot of what we call intelligence is more about the structure of the world than about the particular hardware doing the learning.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that reasoning can be understood as recognizing familiar structure and applying what was learned, making the boundary between pattern fitting and understanding blurry.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not distinguish learning patterns of orbital motion from having a causal model of gravity.

astra-6.text:
I think that claim assumes we know more about human intelligence than we actually do. We recognize patterns, we learn from experience, and we generalize from what we’ve seen. So saying that a neural network is “just fitting patterns” doesn’t, by itself, establish a fundamental difference. A lot depends on what you mean by a pattern.

If you mean memorizing examples and reproducing them, then sure, that’s a limited account of intelligence. But learning patterns can also mean discovering structure that lets you solve problems you’ve never encountered before. That’s a much more interesting capability.

To me, the question is where these systems generalize well and where they fail. Can they adapt to a new situation? Can they learn efficiently? Those are concrete things we can investigate. I wouldn’t assume that deep learning works the same way as the human brain, but I also wouldn’t rule it out as a route to intelligence just because we can describe its training as fitting patterns.

r001.rationale: The candidate says humans recognize patterns, learn from experience, and generalize, so describing neural networks as fitting patterns does not itself establish a fundamental difference.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not distinguish learning patterns of orbital motion from having a causal model of gravity.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m not sure that “it only fits patterns” is a very useful distinction. Humans learn patterns, too. If you’ve seen a lot of examples of something and you can use that experience to handle a new situation, you could describe that as pattern matching. But that description doesn’t tell you much about the richness of the representation you’ve learned or the reasoning you’re doing with it.

The interesting question is what happens when you move beyond the situations you trained on. Can you generalize? Can you build an abstraction and apply it somewhere else? Can you figure out how the world would change if you took a particular action? Those are concrete capabilities we can investigate in both people and neural networks.

I think there are real differences between current deep learning systems and human intelligence. But calling one “pattern fitting” and the other “understanding” can assume the conclusion. We need to be more specific about what the system can do, where it fails, and what would explain that failure.

r001.rationale: The response says humans learn patterns too and that using experience to handle new situations can be described as pattern matching.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss orbital motion or distinguish pattern learning from a causal model of gravity.
